transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Riverside Community Centre. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Hello. I saw some information about your evening courses and I'd like to enrol on one, if there are still places.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Of course. Which course were you interested in?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Well, I was originally thinking about the watercolour painting course, but I've just read that it's full. So I'd like to try the introduction to pottery instead.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Pottery - yes, we've got a few places left on that one. It runs on two different evenings. The Tuesday group is completely full, I'm afraid, but there's space on Wednesday evenings.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Wednesday's fine. Actually, that suits me better.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Great. Let me take some details. Can I have your name, please?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Yes, it's Helen Thornbury.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Could you spell the surname for me?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: T-H-O-R-N-B-U-R-Y.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Thank you. And your address?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: It's 14 Marsh Lane, and the postcode is BS7 2LQ.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: BS7... sorry, was that 2LQ?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: That's right. L for London, Q for Queen.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Lovely. And a contact phone number?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: My mobile is best. It's 07723 418 590.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: 07723 418 590. And can I ask how you heard about the course? We're trying to find out which of our advertising works.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Well, a friend did mention that you run classes, but it was actually a poster in the library that made me ring.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: The library - that's good to know. Now, the fee. The full price for the ten-week course is one hundred and sixty pounds.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Oh, right.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: But do you live in the borough?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Yes, I do - Marsh Lane is just round the corner.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: In that case you're entitled to the residents' rate, which is one hundred and forty-five pounds.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: That's better. Does that include materials?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Yes, the clay and the firing are all included. The only thing you'll need to bring yourself is an apron, because it can get quite messy.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: I've got an old one somewhere. What time do classes start?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Most of our evening classes begin at seven, but pottery starts a little earlier, at a quarter to seven, so that there's time to clean up at the end.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Six forty-five. OK. And is there anywhere to park? I'll probably drive.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: The car park at the front of the centre is for staff only, I'm afraid, but there's free parking behind the supermarket, which is about two minutes' walk away.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Perfect. Thank you so much.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hartwell Nature Reserve. My name's Sam Price, and I coordinate the volunteer programme here. Thank you all for giving up your time - we genuinely couldn't manage the reserve without people like you.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: Let me start with a little background. The reserve covers about two hundred hectares, and much of it was farmland until the late 1990s. It was bought by a local trust in 1998, but the visitor centre where we're sitting now only opened in 2006. Before that, the only facility was a small hut by the car park.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: People often ask what makes Hartwell special. We do have some rare plants, and the woodland is lovely in spring, but what really draws visitors from across the region is the wetland. Since we restored the lake and the reed beds, the number of wading birds that spend the winter here has risen enormously, and that's what brings most of our visitors.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: Now, a few practical points. Most of you will be working outdoors, so please do wear sturdy boots. We'll provide gloves and any tools you need, and there are waterproof jackets in the store room if the weather turns - but we don't have boots in every size, so please bring your own.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: Safety is obviously important. If you're working on your own, you must let the office know which area you'll be in before you set off. You don't need to carry a radio - mobile coverage is fine across most of the reserve - but we do need to know where you are.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: As for refreshments, the cafe in the visitor centre gives all volunteers a free hot drink, and you'll get ten per cent off food. Please don't use the staff kitchen, though - it's very small and it's reserved for the rangers.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: Right, let me tell you about this month's main activities and when they happen. Bird counting is something many of you were interested in. We do our main survey early on Saturday mornings, when the birds are most active and the paths are quiet.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: Path maintenance is a big job after the wet winter. We tried doing it at weekends, but there were too many visitors around, so it now happens on Mondays, when the reserve is closed to the public.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: Then there's hedge planting. That's on Wednesdays, because that's the day the trust's tree nursery can deliver the young plants. Guiding school groups along the children's discovery trail obviously has to fit in with the schools, and most of them visit midweek, so that's also on Wednesdays.

transcript.speaker: Sam Price
transcript.text: And finally, litter picking around the lake. Sadly, that's needed most when the reserve is at its busiest, so we do it on Saturdays, at the end of the day after the visitors have gone home.

sections.title: Tutorial: a presentation on canteen food waste

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your presentation on food waste?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Yes, we've done most of the research, but we wanted to check a few things with you.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Fine. Remind me what your main focus is.

transcript.speaker: Leo
transcript.text: We're looking at food waste in the university's own canteens - how much is thrown away, and why.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: And how did you collect your data?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: We'd planned to interview the kitchen staff, but they were too busy during term, so in the end we weighed the waste ourselves at the end of each lunch service for two weeks. We also ran an online survey of students.

transcript.speaker: Leo
transcript.text: We thought about putting cameras in the dining hall to see what people left on their plates, but there were privacy issues.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Sensible. So what did you find were the main causes?

transcript.speaker: Leo
transcript.text: The biggest one, by far, was portion size. Students said the standard portions were simply too large, especially at lunchtime.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: And the second thing that came up again and again was that people bought food and then didn't like it - particularly new dishes on the menu that they hadn't tried before. Price didn't seem to matter much, and surprisingly few people complained about the quality of the food.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Interesting. What about the structure of the presentation? You've got fifteen minutes.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: We were going to start with the statistics, but we think that might be a bit dry. So we're going to open with a short video clip of the bins at the end of one lunch service.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: That would certainly get people's attention.

transcript.speaker: Leo
transcript.text: The problem is that the clip is quite long.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Then cut it down. Thirty seconds is plenty. And after that?

transcript.speaker: Leo
transcript.text: We'll explain our method, then the findings, then our recommendations. I think the canteens should offer two portion sizes - a smaller portion at a lower price. Some universities already do this.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: And I'd like to suggest free tasting samples of new dishes, so people can try them before they buy.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Both sound practical. But I'd be careful about the claim in your draft that waste could be cut by half. Where does that figure come from?

transcript.speaker: Leo
transcript.text: It's from a study at a university in Canada.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: One study isn't enough to support such a definite claim. You can mention it, but present it as an example of what happened in one place, not as a prediction for us.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: OK, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Who are you expecting in the audience?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Mainly students from our course, but the catering manager has said she'll come.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Then make sure your recommendations are realistic. She'll know exactly what's possible in those kitchens. And how many slides have you got?

transcript.speaker: Leo
transcript.text: About twenty at the moment.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: That's far too many for fifteen minutes. Aim for eight or nine, and put the detailed tables in a handout.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Before you go, I wanted to ask about your sources. You used the government report on food waste?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Yes, but it was published more than ten years ago, so a lot of the figures are out of date.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: And the article by the environmental scientist?

transcript.speaker: Leo
transcript.text: That was really hard going - it was full of chemistry about how food breaks down. Much too technical for what we needed.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: What about the documentary?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: That's actually what made us choose this topic in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: And the canteen's own records?

transcript.speaker: Leo
transcript.text: They were the best thing we had. They gave us exact figures for how much food was ordered every week.

transcript.speaker: Dr Ellis
transcript.text: Good. Well, it sounds as if you're in good shape.

sections.title: Lecture: the history of the pencil

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Today I want to look at an object so ordinary that most of us never think about it: the pencil. Its story begins in the sixteenth century in Borrowdale, a valley in the north of England, where a large deposit of a soft, black and unusually pure mineral was discovered. Local shepherds quickly found a use for it - they used it to mark their sheep, so that everyone could tell whose animals were whose.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: At the time, nobody understood what the substance actually was. Because it left a dark mark rather like lead does, people assumed it was a form of lead, and that's why, even today, we talk about 'pencil lead', although pencils have never contained any lead at all. The mineral is, of course, graphite, which is a form of carbon.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Borrowdale graphite soon became extremely valuable - not only for writing, but also for lining the moulds that were used to make cannonballs. As a result, the mine was closely guarded, and at one stage the workers were searched as they left each day, to make sure that nobody was smuggling any graphite out.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Pure graphite was too soft and brittle to use on its own, so it was usually wrapped in string or held in a wooden holder. The big breakthrough came in 1795, when a French scientist, Nicolas-Jacques Conte, found a way of making pencils without pure graphite. He mixed powdered graphite with clay, shaped the mixture into thin rods, and then fired them in a kiln - much as you would with pottery. This process had a huge advantage: by changing the proportion of clay, manufacturers could control how hard the pencil was. The more clay you add, the harder the pencil, and the lighter the line it produces.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, pencils come in many shapes, but the most common is hexagonal. Some people find round pencils more comfortable, but a hexagonal pencil is far less likely to roll off a sloping desk, and it's also cheaper to make, because more pencils can be cut from the same block of wood.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil seems obvious to us now, but the idea wasn't patented until 1858, in the United States. Interestingly, in many European countries pencils are still usually sold without one.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And then there's the colour. Why are so many pencils yellow? In the 1890s, one manufacturer painted its pencils yellow to suggest that its graphite came from China, because in China yellow was associated with royalty, and so with quality. The idea caught on, and yellow became the standard colour for pencils in North America.

passages.title: Stone upon Stone: The Craft of Dry-Stone Walling

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has walked through the hill country of northern Britain will have noticed them: grey walls running for kilometres across the slopes, climbing hills that seem too steep to farm and disappearing into the mist. These walls contain no cement or mortar of any kind. Each one is held together by nothing more than the careful placement of stones and the force of gravity. Built mostly between the late eighteenth and mid-nineteenth centuries, when common land was being divided into private fields, many of them are still standing two hundred years later, which says a great deal about the skill of the people who made them.

A dry-stone wall is, in fact, two walls leaning against each other. The builder, known as a waller, begins by digging a shallow trench and laying the largest stones, called footings, along the bottom. Two faces of stone are then raised side by side, each sloping slightly inwards - a shape that wallers call the 'batter'. The gap between the faces is packed tightly with small, irregular pieces known as hearting, which prevent the outer stones from moving. At regular intervals, long 'through stones' are laid across the full width of the wall to tie the two faces together. Finally, a row of upright stones, the coping, is placed along the top, its weight pressing the whole structure down.

Wallers follow a number of rules, passed on from one generation to the next. The most important is 'one over two, two over one': every stone should sit across a joint in the row below, never directly on top of another joint, so that weight is spread evenly. Stones are also laid with their length going into the wall rather than along it, a principle that feels wasteful to beginners, who naturally want to cover as much distance as possible. An experienced waller rarely picks up the same stone twice, judging at a glance where each piece will fit. Even so, progress is slow: a skilled individual with a good supply of local stone might complete around five metres of wall in a day.

For much of the twentieth century, the craft declined. Farm labour became expensive, and wire fences, which could be put up in a fraction of the time, replaced walls on many farms. Walls that collapsed were often left as heaps of stone, and the number of people able to repair them fell sharply. By the 1970s, some observers feared that the knowledge would disappear altogether within a generation.

The situation began to change when conservation groups and landowners recognised that the walls were more than just boundaries. Their cracks and crevices provide shelter for insects, small mammals and nesting birds, while the lichens and mosses that grow on the stones support further life. Walls also protect livestock from wind and snow, something a wire fence cannot offer. Grants were introduced to help farmers pay for repairs, and training courses and competitions helped to raise the profile of the craft. Today, professional wallers can earn a reasonable living, and many report that demand for their services is greater than the number of skilled people available.

Interest has also grown among people with no connection to farming. Garden designers use dry-stone techniques to create features that blend into the landscape, and weekend courses regularly attract office workers looking for a physical, outdoor contrast to their working lives. Some engineers argue that the walls offer lessons for modern construction: because they are built without mortar, they can flex slightly as the ground moves, and their stones can be reused again and again. Critics point out, however, that such methods are too slow and labour-intensive to be practical for most building projects.

Whatever their future role, dry-stone walls remain one of the most recognisable features of the upland landscape. As one waller put it, 'A good wall is a conversation between the builder and the hillside - and if you listen properly, the hillside tells you where every stone should go.'

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Yawning is one of the most widespread behaviours in the animal kingdom. Fish yawn, birds yawn, and almost every mammal that has been studied yawns, from mice to elephants. Humans begin remarkably early: ultrasound scans have shown babies yawning in the womb from around eleven weeks after conception, long before they have any experience of tiredness or boredom. A behaviour so common, and so ancient, is likely to serve some purpose - and yet scientists are still debating what that purpose is.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For many years, the most widely accepted explanation was that yawning brings extra oxygen into the body, or removes excess carbon dioxide, when breathing has become shallow. The theory seemed to fit everyday experience: people yawn in stuffy rooms and at the end of long, inactive days. When it was finally tested, however, it did not survive. In experiments carried out in the 1980s, volunteers breathed air containing unusually high levels of carbon dioxide, or pure oxygen, and the frequency of their yawning did not change at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more recent idea is that yawning helps to cool the brain. A deep yawn draws in a large volume of air and stretches the jaw, which increases blood flow to the head; together, these may carry away excess heat. Supporters of the theory point to studies showing that people yawn more often when the surrounding air is moderate in temperature than when it is very hot or very cold - exactly what would be expected if yawning works best when the incoming air is cooler than the body. In another study, volunteers who held a cold pack against their forehead yawned far less than those who held a warm one.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whatever its original function, yawning has another striking feature: it is contagious. Around half of all adults will yawn after watching someone else do so, and for some people even reading about yawning - as you may be discovering now - is enough to set them off. Interestingly, very young children rarely catch yawns. The tendency usually appears at about the age of four or five, around the time children start to understand that other people have thoughts and feelings different from their own.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This timing has led some researchers to suggest that contagious yawning is linked to empathy. In support of this view, studies have found that yawns spread more readily between family members than between friends, and more readily between friends than between strangers. Contagious yawning has also been observed in other social animals, including chimpanzees, and some experiments suggest that pet dogs may even catch yawns from their owners.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Many questions remain unanswered. If yawning does cool the brain, it may help us to stay alert, which would explain why people often yawn just before an important event rather than only when they are tired: athletes before a race, musicians before a performance and parachutists before a jump have all been seen yawning. Some scientists now see the yawn as a signal that the body is moving from one state to another - from sleep to waking, or from rest to action. If they are right, the humble yawn may be less a sign of boredom than a way of getting ready.

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the car shaped the modern city. Roads were widened, junctions were redesigned to keep traffic flowing, and new neighbourhoods were built on the assumption that every household would drive. Walking, meanwhile, came to be treated as a leftover activity - something people did in the short gaps between the car park and the front door. In recent years, however, a growing number of planners have argued that this order of priorities should be reversed, and that a city which is pleasant to walk in is likely to be healthier, more prosperous and more sociable than one built around the car.

The health argument is the easiest to make. Regular walking reduces the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and depression, and, unlike going to a gym, it can be built into daily routines without extra time or expense. Studies in several countries have found that people who live in neighbourhoods where shops, schools and parks are within easy reach on foot tend to be more physically active than those in car-dependent suburbs, even when differences in income and age are taken into account. It would be a mistake, though, to assume that people will walk simply because walking is good for them; most choose to walk only when it is the most convenient way of getting where they want to go.

The economic case is less obvious but, to my mind, equally strong. Shopkeepers frequently oppose plans to remove parking spaces or close streets to traffic, believing that most of their customers arrive by car. When such changes have been made, though, the results have often surprised them. Pedestrians tend to spend less per visit than drivers, but they visit more often, and over a month they frequently spend more in total. Streets with wide pavements, trees and places to sit also encourage people to linger, and lingering customers are good for business.

What, then, makes a place walkable? Distance matters, but so does the quality of the journey. People will happily walk a kilometre along a lively street with shop windows, other pedestrians and occasional places to rest, yet they will avoid a walk of half that length beside a busy road with narrow pavements and long waits at crossings. Small details can have a disproportionate effect: the length of time a pedestrian light stays green, the presence of shade on hot days, or simply whether the most direct route is blocked by a fence.

Critics of the walkable-city movement raise some reasonable objections. They point out that not everyone can walk long distances, and that older people, disabled people and parents with young children may depend on cars more than others. They also warn that improving a neighbourhood can push up property prices, forcing out the very residents who were supposed to benefit. These concerns deserve to be taken seriously, but I do not believe they are arguments against walkable design itself. Rather, they show that it must be combined with good public transport and with policies that protect affordable housing.

Perhaps the most encouraging lesson from cities that have made progress is that change does not need to be dramatic or expensive. Temporary measures - painting a car-free area on a road, placing benches and planters in a former parking space, or closing a street to traffic on Sundays - allow residents to experience the difference before permanent decisions are made. In many cases, initial opposition has faded once people have seen the results for themselves. Such trials also give planners valuable information about how people actually behave, which is not always what their models predict.

None of this means that cars will disappear from cities, nor should it. Deliveries, emergency services and many individual journeys will continue to depend on them. The question is not whether to ban the car, but how much space and priority it should be given. For decades the answer was 'as much as possible'. A more balanced answer, I would argue, is long overdue.
